transcript: Your mobile app sends every API call in plain text. So someone on the same coffee shop Wi-Fi just watched all of your users log in. So your user opens your app at a coffee shop. Every request between the app and your server crosses the network where anyone on that Wi-Fi can read it. Login credentials, session tokens, personal data. An attacker running a free tool on the same network captures all of it without touching your server or your app at all. So let's get this thing locked down. Step one, your app is not verifying the server it's talking to. So your AI set up the API connection but never pinned the certificate. An attacker on the same network can sit between your app and your server, An attacker on the same network can sit between your app and your server, intercept every single request, and your app will never know the difference at all. So, direct your AI to implement certificate pinning so your app only communicates with your verified server. That, and it rejects any connection where the certificate does not match.That's a win. Step two, sensitive data is traveling in the request body with no additional protection. Even with a secure connection, tokens and credentials sitting in plain text in the request body are one misconfiguration away from full exposure. So direct your AI to encrypt sensitive fields in your API payloads independently of the transport layer. That so the data is protected even if the connection is compromised. And step three, your app stores credentials on the device in plain text. So your AI saved the authentication token in local storage where any other app or anyone with physical access to the device can read it. So direct your ad and move all tokens and credentials into the platform's secure storage. So they are encrypted at rest and inaccessible to other applications. And, well, your app works. Your connection is not secure. That's the problem. So fix that transport layer before your users end up paying for it.

claims.topic: Mobile application API transport security, payload protection, and credential storage
claims.problem: The transcript asserts that the mobile app's API communication and credential handling are insecure: API calls and sensitive data are allegedly readable to attackers on the same Wi-Fi network, server identity validation is inadequate, sensitive request-body fields lack protection beyond the transport layer, and credentials are stored on-device in plaintext.
technicalClaims: Claim: API calls are allegedly sent in plaintext or otherwise readable on the network, so an attacker on the same coffee-shop Wi-Fi can passively capture login credentials, session tokens, and personal data without compromising the server or modifying the app.

Claim: Server authentication is allegedly inadequate because the app does not pin the server certificate; a same-network attacker could perform a man-in-the-middle interception, and the app would not detect that it is not communicating with the verified server.

Claim: Sensitive data in API request bodies allegedly has no protection independent of the transport layer; even if a secure connection is intended, plaintext tokens and credentials in the body are described as being one transport misconfiguration or compromised connection away from exposure.
Claim: Credentials or authentication tokens are allegedly stored on the device in plaintext local storage, making them readable by other applications or by someone with physical access to the device.
claims.recommendedSolution: Treat the proposed remediation as a hypothesis to verify in the repository and runtime environment: implement certificate pinning so the app communicates only with the intended verified server and rejects certificate mismatches; encrypt sensitive fields in API payloads independently of the transport layer; move all tokens and credentials from plaintext local storage into the platform's secure storage; and prioritize fixing the transport-layer security problem before release or continued production use.
reasoning: If API requests are transmitted in plaintext or are otherwise readable to local-network observers, then anyone on the same Wi-Fi can inspect traffic and capture credentials, session tokens, and personal data with packet-capture tools, without needing server or app access.

If the app does not adequately verify the server identity and does not pin the expected certificate or public key, then a same-network attacker may be able to sit between the app and server, terminate or intercept traffic, and present a certificate the app accepts; certificate pinning is proposed to change that mechanism by rejecting connections whose certificate does not match the expected server identity.

If sensitive credentials or tokens are merely placed as plaintext fields in API payloads, then their confidentiality depends entirely on correct transport security configuration; independent field-level encryption is proposed to reduce exposure if the transport layer is misconfigured or compromised.

If tokens or credentials are written to generic local storage in plaintext, then device compromise, physical access, or cross-application access could expose them; platform secure storage is proposed to protect them with encryption at rest and OS-level access controls.
assumptions: The mobile app handles login credentials, session tokens, or comparable sensitive personal data.
The app communicates with a backend API over networks that may include untrusted public Wi-Fi.

The alleged plaintext API traffic, missing certificate pinning, plaintext request-body sensitive fields, and plaintext local credential storage are present in the actual codebase or deployed configuration.
The target mobile platforms provide secure credential storage APIs suitable for the app's authentication tokens and credentials.

Certificate pinning can be deployed without breaking required operational practices such as certificate rotation, CDN/proxy use, or environment-specific backend endpoints, or those practices can be accommodated safely.
Field-level encryption can be implemented with sound key management; otherwise encrypting payload fields may not provide the intended protection.
Attackers in scope include local-network observers or man-in-the-middle actors, and potentially other apps or people with physical access to the device.
technologiesAndPatterns: Packet capture or network sniffing on public Wi-Fi
Platform secure storage / secure credential store

implications.detail: Credentials, session tokens, and personal data may be exposed to passive local-network attackers if API traffic is actually plaintext or otherwise readable.

Lack of certificate pinning, as framed by the transcript, may allow man-in-the-middle interception if the app accepts an attacker-controlled certificate or otherwise fails to detect an unexpected server identity.
Sensitive request fields without protection beyond transport security may be exposed by a TLS or configuration failure, according to the transcript's threat model.
Plaintext token or credential storage may allow credential theft from the device through physical access, device compromise, or inappropriate cross-application access.
Certificate pinning introduces an operational dependency on certificate or key rotation practices because mismatches are intended to cause connection rejection.
Adding independent payload encryption and secure storage changes authentication and API-client code paths and requires consistent handling across all sensitive fields and token lifecycle operations.

uncertainties: Repository inspection can check whether API base URLs use plaintext HTTP, whether TLS is configured, whether certificate pinning or equivalent trust restrictions are implemented, and whether sensitive fields are sent in request payloads.

Repository inspection can check whether tokens or credentials are written to generic local storage, shared preferences, files, SQLite, WebView storage, or another plaintext-accessible persistence mechanism instead of platform secure storage.

Repository inspection can identify use of platform secure storage APIs and field-level encryption libraries, but correct runtime protection also depends on key management, OS configuration, device state, and deployment environment.

Whether a same-Wi-Fi attacker can actually capture credentials or tokens depends on the deployed transport configuration, certificate validation behavior, network conditions, proxy behavior, and whether sensitive values are present in observed traffic.

The transcript equates lack of certificate pinning with the app not verifying the server; in many platforms default TLS certificate validation may still occur without pinning, so an audit should distinguish absence of pinning from absence of all server certificate validation while preserving the transcript's stated concern.
The claim that other apps can read locally stored credentials depends on the storage mechanism, mobile OS sandboxing, device compromise state, backups, debug settings, and file permissions.

The effectiveness and necessity of field-level payload encryption depend on the threat model and whether transport-layer security is correctly enforced; the repository alone may not prove whether it is required or sufficient.

onboardingPrompt:
You are performing a read-only architecture onboarding for a mobile application repository. Do not edit files, generate implementation code, create commits, or recommend fixes yet. Your job is to discover the current system so a follow-up audit can evaluate specific security claims. Do not assume any vulnerability exists. Separate confirmed repository facts from inference and unknowns, and cite exact evidence.

Focus on mobile API communication, handling of sensitive request/response data, authentication/session state, and on-device persistence. Adapt your exploration to the actual stack you find: native iOS/Swift/Obj-C, native Android/Kotlin/Java, React Native, Flutter/Dart, Xamarin/.NET, Capacitor/Cordova, shared SDK modules, generated API clients, or other frameworks. If this repo contains only part of the system, identify boundaries and missing components.

Discovery tasks:

1. Repository and runtime shape
- Identify apps, packages/modules, platforms, build variants/flavors/schemes, environment folders, generated clients, shared networking libraries, and test targets.
- Locate dependency manifests and security-relevant libraries: HTTP clients, GraphQL/REST clients, auth SDKs, storage libraries, crypto libraries, WebView/native bridge components, certificate/trust/network policy configuration, analytics/crash/logging SDKs.
- Note where production, staging, development, and local endpoints are configured. Include build-time flags, remote config, feature flags, environment variables, plist/xml/json/yaml/gradle files, CI injection, or generated configuration.

2. API transport and request flow map
- Trace how an authenticated API request is built and sent from UI/business action to network layer and back: routes/endpoints, base URL selection, interceptors/middleware, headers, cookies, authorization fields, retry logic, redirects, proxy settings, WebView calls, background jobs, uploads/downloads, and error handling.
- Identify all HTTP client instances and any custom configuration for protocols, timeouts, TLS/trust behavior, hostname verification, cleartext allowances, debug proxies, logging interceptors, request/response inspection, and environment-specific overrides.
- Capture representative flows for login, token refresh, account/profile data, and any other sensitive operations discovered in the code. Provide file paths and exact classes/functions/config keys.

3. Sensitive data inventory and lifecycle
- Identify types of sensitive data the app appears to handle: credentials, session/access/refresh tokens, API keys, personal data, device identifiers, payment/health/location data, or comparable fields. Do not infer beyond evidence.
- Map where these values originate, how they enter request bodies/headers/query params, how responses are parsed, and where values are held in memory, cached, logged, serialized, or persisted.
- Locate request/response models, serializers, GraphQL operations, OpenAPI/generated schemas, DTOs, form encoders, and custom body builders. Note field names that appear sensitive and the routes using them.

4. On-device persistence and credential state
- Inventory persistence mechanisms in use: platform preferences/defaults, key/value storage, files, SQLite/Room/Core Data/Realm/Hive/MMKV/AsyncStorage/SecureStore/Keychain/Keystore wrappers, WebView/localStorage, cookies, caches, backups, and debug data stores.
- Trace token/credential lifecycle: creation/login, storage, reads for API authorization, refresh, logout/revocation, migration, expiration, and deletion. Include concrete symbols and call sites.
- Identify wrappers/abstractions around storage and any platform-specific implementations.

5. Platform security configuration and operational context
- Map Android network security config, manifest flags, backup/debuggable settings, cleartext settings, permissions, exported components, and build-type differences relevant to network/storage behavior.
- Map iOS App Transport Security settings, entitlements, keychain/access group usage, associated domains, debug/proxy flags, and build scheme differences relevant to network/storage behavior.
- For cross-platform apps, identify native bridge modules and whether platform-specific security behavior diverges.
- Note CI/CD, release signing, configuration generation, and test fixtures if they influence endpoint or storage behavior.

6. Tests and observability
- Identify existing unit/integration/e2e tests covering network client configuration, auth flows, token persistence, logout, serialization, and platform-specific storage.
- Identify logging, crash reporting, analytics, network debugging, redaction utilities, and test/dev-only instrumentation that may expose or protect sensitive values. Distinguish production from debug behavior.

Evidence requirements:
- For each fact, provide file path, symbol name, route/schema/config key/test name, and a short explanation of what it proves.
- Label items as Confirmed, Inferred, or Unknown. If evidence is generated or indirect, say so.
- Do not run destructive commands. If you run tests or static searches, report commands and results; do not require runtime traffic capture in this onboarding unless already available.

Deliverable:
Provide a concise architecture briefing with: repository shape, technology stack, security-relevant boundaries, API request/control/data-flow diagrams in text form, sensitive data lifecycle map, storage map, environment/configuration map, tests/observability summary, and key unknowns. End with a short handoff map listing the exact files/symbols/configs the follow-up audit should inspect first. Then STOP and wait for the next prompt.
investigationPrompt:
You are now performing a read-only, claim-specific security investigation of a mobile application repository. Do not edit files, implement fixes, write commits, or refactor. Use the prior architecture briefing if available, but verify all material facts directly from repository evidence. Where runtime proof would be required, state exactly what evidence is missing; do not fabricate packet captures, logs, traces, metrics, or device behavior.

Investigation hypothesis to test:
The video claims that the app’s API transport and credential handling may be insecure. The proposed remediation, to be assessed rather than assumed correct, is: enforce communication only with the intended verified server using certificate/public-key pinning or an equivalent trust restriction; encrypt sensitive API payload fields independently of the transport layer; move all tokens/credentials from plaintext local storage to platform secure storage; and prioritize transport-layer fixes before release or continued production use. Important qualifications: absence of pinning is not the same as absence of TLS certificate validation on modern mobile platforms; field-level encryption only helps with sound key management and a threat model that justifies it; local storage exposure depends on OS sandboxing, backups, device compromise, debug state, permissions, and storage mechanism; operational practices such as certificate rotation, CDNs/proxies, environment endpoints, and debugging requirements may constrain solution fit.

Use these applicability statuses for every material claim and subclaim: Confirmed, Partially Applicable, Refuted, Not Applicable, or Needs Runtime Verification. For each status include exact static evidence, missing evidence, assumptions, realistic impact, severity if meaningful, and confidence. Severity must be Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Informational based on actual exposure, frequency, scale, exploitability, reliability, and operational cost. Do not exaggerate a theoretical concern into a production issue.

Scope and evidence rules:
- Static repository evidence can establish code paths, configuration, dependency choices, allowed protocols, storage APIs, serializers, tests, and build-variant differences.
- Runtime evidence is required to prove actual over-the-air readability, successful same-Wi-Fi interception, deployed certificate behavior, production endpoint behavior, device backup/sandbox exposure, key material availability at runtime, and traffic contents under real credentials.
- Cite file paths, exact symbols/classes/functions, config keys, manifest/plist/xml entries, routes, schema/model names, tests, generated client locations, and relevant line references if available.
- If code is platform-specific, analyze Android and iOS separately and then summarize combined app exposure. If the repo is cross-platform, include native bridge implementations and per-platform configuration.

Recommended methodology and report sections:

1. Sensitive asset and attack-surface baseline
- Inventory the sensitive values actually handled by the app: login credentials, access tokens, refresh tokens, cookies, session IDs, personal data, device identifiers, or other regulated/sensitive fields. Tie each value to routes, models, headers/body/query fields, and persistence locations.
- Identify attacker models that are applicable from code evidence: passive local-network observer, active MITM, malicious local app, physical access, rooted/jailbroken device, debug build user, backup extractor. Mark unsupported attacker models as assumptions.
- Determine production vs debug/staging behavior. Distinguish test fixtures, mock servers, sample apps, and development-only bypasses from release code.

2. Claim A — API calls are plaintext or otherwise passively readable on the network
Evaluate whether repository evidence supports passive same-network readability without app/server compromise.
Checks to perform:
- Enumerate all API base URLs and endpoint construction paths. Identify scheme (`http://` vs `https://`), environment overrides, remote config, hardcoded hosts, WebView endpoints, generated clients, deep-link/API bridge calls, and fallback URLs.
- Inspect Android Network Security Config, manifest `usesCleartextTraffic`, per-domain cleartext policies, debug overrides, OkHttp/Retrofit/Ktor/WebView settings, and logging/debug proxy interceptors. Inspect iOS ATS exceptions, arbitrary loads, domain exceptions, URLSession/Alamofire/WKWebView behavior, and build-scheme differences.
- Trace whether credentials/tokens/personal data appear in URL query strings, headers, or bodies for login, refresh, and sensitive operations. Query strings and logs have different exposure properties than TLS-protected request bodies.
- Identify any code that disables TLS, accepts all certificates, uses insecure protocols, permits mixed content, downgrades to HTTP, or sends sensitive data to non-API third parties.
Applicability guidance:
- `http://` production endpoints carrying sensitive data may support Confirmed or High/Critical findings depending on reachability and frequency.
- HTTPS with normal platform validation generally refutes passive plaintext capture but may still need runtime verification for deployment/configuration.
- Debug-only HTTP/mock endpoints should not be treated as production exposure unless build controls are weak.
Required output: status, evidence table, affected routes/assets, production/debug distinction, runtime tests needed such as packet capture on release build, proxy observation, server config validation, or deployed app config verification.

3. Claim B — Server identity validation is inadequate because certificate pinning is absent; MITM would not be detected
Investigate the causal chain carefully: server identity validation, trust anchors, hostname verification, custom trust managers/delegates, and whether pinning/equivalent restrictions exist.
Checks to perform:
- Locate all HTTP client trust configuration: custom `TrustManager`, `HostnameVerifier`, `SSLSocketFactory`, OkHttp `CertificatePinner`, Android network security trust anchors, iOS `URLSessionDelegate`/`SecTrust` handling, Alamofire `ServerTrustManager`, React Native/Flutter plugin configuration, WebView certificate callbacks, and third-party SDK clients if configurable.
- Identify code that accepts all certificates, bypasses hostname validation, ignores TLS errors, trusts user-added CAs in release, or includes debug CA overrides in production. These are stronger evidence of MITM risk than absence of pinning alone.
- Identify existing certificate/public-key pinning, certificate transparency, private CA restrictions, mTLS, allowlisted trust anchors, domain-scoped policies, or backend/API gateway controls that alter risk.
- Evaluate operational constraints: certificate rotation, public key vs leaf certificate pinning, backup pins, CDN/proxy/TLS termination, multiple environments, disaster recovery, app update cadence, kill switches/remote config, enterprise proxies, and support burden.
Applicability guidance:
- Absence of pinning alone should not be reported as “no server verification.” Most mobile TLS stacks validate CA chain and hostname by default; classify as Partially Applicable or Informational/Medium only if the threat model requires resistance to compromised/user-installed CAs or active MITM beyond default TLS.
- Any release code accepting all certs or disabling hostname verification can elevate severity substantially.
- If pinning exists but is incomplete by host/platform/build, report partial coverage.
Required output: distinguish default TLS validation from pinning; list exact trust behavior evidence; identify active MITM scenarios actually supported by static evidence; state runtime verification needed, such as controlled proxy MITM against a release build and validation of installed trust stores.

4. Claim C — Sensitive request-body fields lack protection independent of transport
Assess whether sensitive fields are sent as plaintext application data inside otherwise protected requests, and whether independent field-level protection exists or is warranted.
Checks to perform:
- Inventory sensitive request fields in login, token refresh, profile update, payment/PII, upload, and telemetry routes. Cite DTOs, serializers, GraphQL variables, form encoders, and generated API schemas.
- Determine whether fields are protected only by transport, protected by application-layer encryption/signing/tokenization, transformed into one-time credentials, or never sent in raw form. Include key derivation and key storage evidence if field protection exists.
- Inspect logging/interceptor/redaction behavior for bodies and headers. Field-level plaintext in code is less concerning if never logged and only sent via validated TLS; more concerning if logged, cached, stored, or sent to analytics/crash tools.
- Evaluate key management feasibility for proposed field-level encryption: where public keys would come from, rotation, replay protection, server compatibility, error handling, testability, and whether client-side keys would be secrets extractable from the app.
Applicability guidance:
- Transport-layer TLS normally provides confidentiality in transit; lack of field-level encryption is not automatically a vulnerability. Treat it as defense-in-depth whose necessity depends on sensitivity, compliance, backend threat model, TLS reliability, and exposure to intermediaries.
- If sensitive fields are transmitted over HTTP or through disabled TLS validation, this claim’s impact compounds with Claims A/B.
- If field-level encryption is present but key management is weak or static symmetric keys are embedded in the app, report that precisely.
Required output: per-route/field matrix showing field, route, protection mechanism, logs/caches, transport dependency, missing runtime evidence, realistic impact, severity, and confidence.

5. Claim D — Credentials or auth tokens are stored on-device in plaintext local storage
Trace credential/token persistence end to end and assess real local exposure.
Checks to perform:
- Find all writes and reads of credentials, access tokens, refresh tokens, session cookies, API keys, and auth-derived secrets. Include wrapper abstractions and platform implementations.
- Classify storage mechanisms: Android SharedPreferences/DataStore/MMKV/files/SQLite/Room/WebView localStorage/cookies vs EncryptedSharedPreferences/Keystore-backed storage; iOS UserDefaults/files/Core Data/SQLite/Keychain with accessibility class/access group; React Native AsyncStorage/SecureStore/Keychain; Flutter SharedPreferences/SecureStorage/Hive; backup and migration paths.
- Inspect whether sensitive values are encoded only with Base64/JSON/obfuscation rather than encrypted; whether encryption keys are hardcoded, stored adjacent to ciphertext, or Keystore/Keychain-backed; whether values are included in device backups, logs, crash reports, screenshots, clipboard, or debug export files.
- Evaluate logout/token revocation/deletion, refresh rotation, expiration, and migration from older storage. Old migration code and legacy keys may preserve exposure.
- Assess OS sandboxing and access assumptions. Other non-privileged apps generally cannot read another app’s private storage on modern mobile OSes; physical access risk depends on lock state, backup settings, root/jailbreak, debug builds, and file protection classes.
Applicability guidance:
- Release code storing tokens/passwords in generic preferences/files/AsyncStorage/UserDefaults without platform-backed encryption may support Confirmed/High or Medium depending on token power/lifetime and device threat model.
- Short-lived tokens, refresh-token rotation, device binding, encrypted storage, or Keychain/Keystore use reduce severity; hardcoded keys or weak wrappers may only partially mitigate.
Required output: storage lifecycle table with value, write site, read site, storage backend, protection, backup/accessibility behavior, deletion path, exposure scenario, status, severity, and confidence.

6. Cross-claim causal chain and combined risk
- Build a causal-chain matrix: preconditions, repository evidence, runtime evidence needed, attacker capability, exposed asset, blast radius, current mitigations, and residual risk.
- Identify interactions: plaintext HTTP plus body credentials; disabled trust validation plus no pinning; body logging plus sensitive fields; generic storage plus long-lived refresh tokens; debug-only configurations leaking into release.
- Identify counterevidence that lowers risk: HTTPS-only production endpoints, strict ATS/network security policy, no sensitive data in traffic, default TLS validation intact, pinning/equivalent controls already present, secure storage wrappers, short-lived scoped tokens, token binding, backend anomaly detection, redaction, or strong logout/revocation.

7. Solution-fit assessment and safer alternatives
Assess the proposed remediation as a hypothesis, not a mandate.
- Certificate/public-key pinning: determine whether it is applicable and proportionate. Consider using public-key pins with backups, scoped hosts, rotation runbooks, remote-disable risks, monitoring, staging/prod differences, and failure modes. If default TLS is intact and the threat model does not require pinning, recommend against over-scoping.
- Field-level encryption: evaluate whether it meaningfully reduces identified exposure or merely adds complexity. Consider using HTTPS enforcement, HSTS/server hardening, request minimization, tokenization, short-lived one-time credentials, redaction, and backend-side controls as smaller/safer alternatives where appropriate.
- Secure storage: evaluate migration to platform secure storage where plaintext/generic persistence is confirmed. Consider token lifetime reduction, refresh rotation, logout deletion, backup exclusion, Keychain accessibility/Keystore constraints, biometric requirements if relevant, and legacy migration cleanup.
- Transport priority: if actual HTTP or TLS bypass exists in release, prioritize those. If only absence of pinning is found with otherwise correct TLS, calibrate priority accordingly.

Final report format:
1. Executive summary: overall disposition — Proceed, Modify Recommendation, Reject, or Gather More Evidence — with 3–5 evidence-backed reasons.
2. Claim status table: Claim A/B/C/D, applicability status, severity, confidence, key evidence, missing runtime proof.
3. Detailed findings by section above, with exact repository citations and explicit production/debug/build-variant distinctions.
4. Static vs runtime evidence: list what was proven statically and the minimal runtime validation plan needed, such as release-build proxy test, packet capture, API endpoint verification, trust-store manipulation test, storage inspection on device, backup extraction check, or log review. Do not claim results you did not obtain.
5. Current mitigations and constraints, counterevidence, side effects/operational cost of the proposed changes, and smaller/safer alternatives.
6. Areas that should remain untouched because they are unrelated, test-only, third-party generated, or already adequately controlled.
7. Open questions for app/security/backend/operations owners.
End with an explicit STOP. No code changes, implementation code, commits, or refactors.
